_meta.title: Bay Area megaprojects: researched project list
notes: Every figure here came from the listed sources as of the lastVerified date. Items in each project's 'verify' list are known gaps; do not fill them by guessing.
approxCenter values are rough [lon, lat] points for placing a marker only. Real site boundaries must come from official plan documents or parcel data, saved per project with their source.
Program numbers are planned or approved figures, not built totals, unless the note says otherwise.
Summaries and stage notes are written for the map's project panel and can be edited freely.

stages.label: Proposed
stages.meaning: Plan announced or application filed; no formal approvals.
stages.treatment: Outline only (dashed). No fill. Massing, if any, drawn as wireframe.

stages.label: In entitlement
stages.meaning: Formal review underway: EIR, specific plan, hearings, land deal.

stages.label: Entitled
stages.meaning: Approvals in hand; no construction yet.

stages.label: Site work
stages.meaning: Demolition, remediation, grading, utilities or streets underway; no vertical buildings yet.
stages.treatment: Light fill with a site-work cue (e.g., hatch on the parcel).

stages.label: Under construction
stages.meaning: Vertical construction underway on at least one building.

stages.label: Partly built
stages.meaning: Project-level only: some buildings delivered, more planned.
stages.treatment: Per-building: delivered buildings in the complete style, the rest by their own stage.

stages.label: Complete
stages.treatment: Ink, matching the existing city: the project has become part of the map.

stages.label: Paused
stages.meaning: Developer or city has halted work; approvals may remain in force.
stages.treatment: Off-ramp color. Shown as a break in the timeline bar.

stages.label: Distressed
stages.meaning: Default, receivership, failed financing or similar threatens the project.
stages.treatment: Second off-ramp color. Shown as a break in the timeline bar.

projects.name: Candlestick Point
projects.acresNote: OCII describes the approximately 272-acre Candlestick Point area; the 2024 CEQA notice of determination gives 271.6 acres. It includes the former stadium and parking lots, the Alice Griffith housing site and the Candlestick Point State Recreation Area. Older Planning documents (2013–2018) said roughly 281 acres.

program.notes: 2024 Modified Project Variant (OCII, Sept 2024). R&D/office rose from 750,000 to 2,800,000 sq ft after about 2,050,000 sq ft moved from Hunters Point Shipyard Phase 2. Retail is 170,000 sq ft regional plus 134,500 sq ft neighborhood. About 34% of Candlestick's 7,218 homes will be below market rate (OCII), counting workforce homes for households earning 120–160% of AMI; across Candlestick Point and Shipyard Phase 2 together the share is about 32% (3,363 of 10,672). The first phase covers seven city blocks with about 700 homes, 314 of them affordable. The Mayor's office cites 100 acres of parks and open space; OCII's open-space count (105.7 acres) includes the existing State Recreation Area.

projects.developer: FivePoint Holdings, LLC (previously Lennar Urban)
publicPartners: SF Office of Community Investment and Infrastructure (OCII)
projects.stageNote: The Mayor broke ground on Sept 9, 2026 on the first new phase: seven city blocks (four mixed-use residential blocks on Harney Way, two residential blocks on Arelious Walker Drive and a commercial parcel in Candlestick Center) with about 700 homes, 314 of them affordable. Roads and utilities come first (OCII: 2026–2028, then housing and commercial buildings); no building permits have been issued for the blocks yet. The 2024 amendments split the Candlestick build-out into seven major phases instead of three.

projects.summary: The former Candlestick Park stadium site and its parking lots, planned as a bayfront neighborhood of about 7,200 homes, an office and R&D district and about 100 acres of parks. It was planned together with Hunters Point Shipyard until 2024, when the city found the two could no longer be built in concert and let Candlestick go ahead on its own.
projects.massingNotes: Boundary: DataSF Former Redevelopment Agency Project Areas (m288-24sn, ODC-PDDL), feature "Bayview Hunters Point Area B Zone 1" (about 271.1 acres, matching the 2024 notice); don't use the "CP" height district, which leaves out the State Recreation Area. Height limits run 40–420 ft with up to 12 towers (2010/2019 Design for Development) and up to 180 ft in Candlestick Center (2024). Massing: the 2024 height plan traced from Addendum 7 to the FEIR (Aug 2024), Figure 5 (40–85 ft blocks; Candlestick Center parcels to 180 ft under the 2024 Innovation District alternative), with 11 towers from the Design for Development Table 4.2 (170–420 ft over 65- or 85-ft podiums; locations flexible), all illustrative; the completed Alice Griffith buildings are outlined with DBI stories (no official height). The State Recreation Area and parks are not drawn. The 2024 amendment adds an alternative chapter only for Candlestick Center (OCII Resolution 28-2024); tower limits elsewhere (Table 4.2, 170–420 ft) are unchanged.

projects.name: Hunters Point Shipyard
projects.acresNote: Shipyard Phase 2: 421.0 acres per the 2024 CEQA notice of determination and OCII. Phase 2 is all of the shipyard except the Hilltop and Hillside (Phase 1); 2018 Planning Commission items said roughly 402 acres. The whole shipyard peninsula is about 490 acres.

program.notes: Phase 2 program after the 2024 transfer of about 2,050,000 sq ft of R&D/office to Candlestick Point (OCII, Sept 2024); the non-residential total includes 410,000 sq ft of institutional space and 255,000 sq ft of artist studios. About 32% of homes are below market rate across Phase 2 and Candlestick Point together. Phase 1 (Hilltop and Hillside) has a goal of 1,428 homes, 29% (407) affordable, and 26 acres of parks.

projects.developer: FivePoint (previously Lennar Urban)
publicPartners: SF Office of Community Investment and Infrastructure (OCII)
U.S. Navy (owns and cleans up the Phase 2 land)
projects.stageNote: No construction is under way on any Phase 2 parcel: the Navy still owns the land, and it has been retesting parts of it, including Parcel C since Aug 2022, after questions about a Navy contractor's earlier work. The Navy expects to convey Phase 2, except Parcel F, in 2036–2038. Phase 1 on the hilltop is mostly built: OCII's draft annual report counts 767 homes complete by June 30, 2025, 293 of them affordable, and the city's 2026 capital plan has the developer finishing the Hillside roads by 2026 and building about 7 acres of parks in 2026–2030.

projects.summary: The former naval shipyard on San Francisco's southeastern tip. projects.name: Potrero Power Station
projects.acresNote: The Draft EIR (Oct 2018, p. S-2) describes an approximately 29.0-acre site made up of five sub-areas: the 21-acre Power Station sub-area, a 4.8-acre PG&E sub-area, a 2.9-acre Port sub-area, a 0.2-acre Southern sub-area and a small City sub-area. Perkins&Will's ~21 acres matches the Power Station sub-area.

program.notes: Office and lab space, retail, PDR/arts uses, and adaptive reuse of historic Station A.

projects.developer: California Barrel Company LLC (Fifth Space)
projects.stageNote: Partly built. The Sophie Maxwell Building at 1212 Maryland St. (8 stories, 105 homes, 100% affordable) has been built: the city marked its building permit complete on Aug 28, 2026. UCSF's clinical and life sciences building on Block 2 is under construction (Planning Commission, July 2026). On Oct 6, 2026 the Board of Supervisors gave final passage to the amended development agreement and Special Use District, which raise some height limits; they await the Mayor's signature.

projects.name: Pier 70
projects.acresNote: The Port's 28-Acre Site (Draft EIR, Dec 2016, p. S.3), part of the 35-acre Pier 70 Special Use District rezoned in 2017. The wider Pier 70 area is 69 acres.

program.notes: Port: 1,100–2,150 homes on the 28-Acre Site (1,500–3,000 across the Special Use District), 30% affordable, and 6.5 acres of parks (9 acres across the district). Proposition F (2014) allows 1–2 million sq ft of commercial and office space; the EIR studied up to about 2.26 million gsf of office. Buildings 2, 12 and 21 are kept and rehabilitated. A proposal the Port heard in Aug 2026 would add about 600 homes and lower the affordable rate to no less than 20%; it is not approved. Phase 1, as approved in 2018, anticipates about 588 homes.

projects.developer: FC Pier 70, LLC (Brookfield Properties)
projects.stageNote: Building 12's rehabilitation was completed in January 2022, and the Port reports it nearly 90% leased (Aug 2026); it is still the project's only vertical building, and historic Buildings 2 and 21 haven't been rehabilitated. The city and Port accepted the Phase 1 streets in 2024; Phase 1 parks and new buildings haven't started. Phase 1 is in a permitted down-market delay, extended to Dec 26, 2026.

projects.name: Mission Rock
projects.acresNote: Draft EIR (April 2017, p. 2-1): the 28-acre site is the 14.2-acre Seawall Lot 337, a 0.3-acre strip (Parcel P20), the 6.0-acre Pier 48, the existing 2.2-acre China Basin Park and 5.4 acres of streets.

Phase 1 has about 52,000 sq ft of retail; the Port's 2019 approvals call for 241,000–244,800 gsf of active retail and production space at full build-out. Plans also rehabilitate about 261,000 sq ft of Pier 48 and add a parking structure on Block D2.

projects.name: Mission Bay
projects.acresNote: OCII: the Mission Bay North (65 acres) and Mission Bay South (238 acres) redevelopment project areas cover 303 acres between San Francisco Bay and Interstate 280.

program.notes: OCII figures: 2,964 homes (698 affordable) and 6.5 acres of parks in Mission Bay North; 3,571 homes (1,218 affordable) and 34 acres of parks in Mission Bay South. Mission Bay South has 6.1 million sq ft of commercial and institutional space and 429 hotel rooms; Mission Bay North about 200,000 sq ft of commercial space. Includes UCSF's research campus and the Warriors' event center on an approximately 11-acre site. Ordinance 22-26 (Feb 2026) raised Mission Bay South's planned homes from about 3,440 to 3,690, adding 250 affordable homes on Block 4 East. Mission Bay North has no hotel; the 429 hotel rooms are in Mission Bay South.

projects.developer: FOCIL-MB LLC (successor to the original master developer, Catellus Development Corporation)
publicPartners: SF Office of Community Investment and Infrastructure (OCII)
projects.stageNote: Largely built. The last two affordable housing sites are moving: OCII approved 398 affordable homes on Block 4 East in Nov 2025, the Board raised the plan's height and housing limits for it in Feb 2026 (Ordinance 22-26), and the city issued building permits for both buildings in June and Sept 2026. Block 12 West, the last residential site, has no housing entitlement left; OCII and FOCIL propose about 535 homes there, with approvals expected in early 2027. The city's 2026 capital plan expects nine more Mission Bay parks over the next four years.

projects.name: Treasure Island and Yerba Buena Island
projects.acresNote: SF Planning: approximately 400 acres on Treasure Island and Yerba Buena Island. It excludes the 37-acre Job Corps campus and the Coast Guard's part of Yerba Buena Island. The DataSF TI/YBI height districts add up to about 390 acres.

program.notes: 8,000 homes is the development agreement's cap, 271 of them on Yerba Buena Island. The 27.2% affordable requirement (2,173 homes) replaces the 2011 figure of up to 2,400. About 311,000 sq ft of adaptive reuse in historic Buildings 1–3. In Jan 2026 the developer applied to add 1,400–2,800 homes; TIDA heard it as an informational item and it is not approved.

projects.developer: Treasure Island Community Development, LLC (Stockbridge Capital Group, Wilson Meany, Kenwood Investments and Lennar)
projects.stageNote: More than 1,200 homes had been completed by May 2026 (City Administrator). The city has marked permits complete for six buildings since 2022, most recently 490 Avenue of the Palms (148 homes) on March 9, 2026, which TIDA said in Sept 2026 is switching from condominiums to rentals. Major Phase 1 is planned to build out through 2027. Ferry service began March 1, 2022.

projects.name: North Bayshore Master Plan

program.notes: Approved maximums. Up to 5,950 market-rate homes and an estimated 1,050 affordable homes (15%), provided through about 7 acres of land dedication. Open space: about 14.8 acres of dedicated public park land and 11.3 acres of privately owned, publicly accessible open space. Heights: residential 5–15 stories, hotels 10–13. projects.name: Berryessa Flea Market South
projects.acresNote: Ordinance 30646 and the Planning Commission memo (May 28, 2021, p. 1) describe an approximately 61.5-gross-acre site at 1590 Berryessa Road (APNs 254-17-052, -053, -007, -084, -095), south of Berryessa Road next to the Berryessa/North San José BART station. Ordinance 30646, the Flea Market Southside rezoning, comes back to the City Council for final adoption.
The owner withdraws its Planned Development Permit and Tentative Map applications for the site.

projects.summary: The 61.5-acre San José Flea Market site next to the Berryessa/North San José BART station, rezoned in 2021 for up to 3,450 homes and 3.4 million sq ft of offices and shops around a 5-acre urban market for the flea market's vendors, with creekside open space along Coyote and Penitencia creeks. projects.name: Mare Island
projects.acresNote: About 3,131 acres, about 1,302 of them developable, per the City's April 27, 2026 report on the draft new specific plan, which keeps the existing plan's overall boundary (the drawn 2005 plan area measures about 3,090 acres). CEQAnet lists 5,250 acres for the 2003–2005 Amended and Restated Mare Island Specific Plan EIR (SCH 2003092057), which covers the whole former shipyard including wetlands and dredge ponds.

program.notes: Up to 14,000 homes and 14,900–17,000 jobs, as the City estimates for the Mare Island Company's first draft specific plan (Oct 2024); not approved. The City's April 2026 report gives a range of about 9,750 to 14,400 homes and about 895 dormitory units. The City's October 2025 infrastructure assessment used an earlier preliminary plan (Feb 2023): 9,271 homes and about 8.13 million sq ft of commercial uses, built out by about 2063. The draft's mixed-use zones allow up to 85 ft. The October 2024 draft's maximum is about 14,400 homes, including 356 existing, and about 8.22 million sq ft of non-residential space (3.77 million new).

publicPartners: City of Vallejo (specific plan, lead agency)

timeline.event: City Council adopts the Mare Island Specific Plan for the former naval shipyard.
City and Lennar Mare Island sign the development agreement for South Mare Island (about 670 acres).
City issues the notice of preparation for an EIR on an amended and restated specific plan with about 2.7 million more sq ft of development potential.
City circulates the supplemental EIR for the 2005 Amended and Restated Mare Island Specific Plan.
The Mare Island Specific Plan is amended.
City and the Nimitz Group enter an exclusive right to negotiate for about 157 acres of North Mare Island.
City Council consents to the transfer of Lennar's South Mare Island holdings to the Nimitz Group; escrow closes in November 2019.
A CEQA addendum to the specific plan EIRs is prepared for the North Mare Island disposition and development agreement.
City and the Nimitz Group sign the North Mare Island disposition and development agreement (about 157 acres).
Mare Island Company submits the first draft of a new Mare Island Specific Plan (file SPA24-0001), with nine neighborhoods.
City and the Vallejo Flood and Wastewater District publish the final Mare Island Infrastructure Assessment.
City sends the Mare Island Company its consolidated comments on the first draft.
City Council receives an informational update on the specific plan, environmental review, infrastructure planning and development agreements.

City reports that the Mare Island Company has paused its Connolly Street corridor project; the Council has asked the City Attorney to find a mediator for talks between the City and the Vallejo Flood and Wastewater District.
City Council approves the third and final extension of the South Mare Island development agreement, to Sept 11, 2031 (Resolution 138 N.C.).

projects.summary: The former Mare Island Naval Shipyard across the strait from downtown Vallejo, where a new specific plan from the Mare Island Company proposes up to about 14,000 homes in nine neighborhoods around the historic shipyard core. It's in early City review, with no approvals yet.

projects.name: Middlefield Park
projects.acresNote: The City Council report of Nov 15, 2022 (p. 2) gives an approximately 40-acre site of 14 parcels. The 14 parcels in the city's parcel layer add up to about 39.8 acres.

Instead of on-site below-market-rate units, Google dedicates 2.4 acres (parcels R4A and R6) to the City for affordable housing, which the applicant estimates at 380 units (20%); a City staff example came to 338 (17%). Open space: 6.97 acres of public parks dedicated to the City plus 2.87 acres of privately owned, publicly accessible open space (Ellis Park).

Environmental Planning Commission recommends approval of the master plan.
City Council certifies the supplemental EIR (Res. 18733), approves the master plan (Res. 18734) and vesting tentative map (Res. 18735), and introduces the development agreement ordinance.
City Council adopts the development agreement (Ordinance 19.22) on second reading, 6–0 with one recusal.
The development agreement takes effect.
City Council approves business terms for a seven-year City lease of 485 and 495 Clyde Ave from Google for a park and pickleball courts, with an option for Google to sell the land to the City.

projects.summary: Google's approved plan to replace 23 low-rise office and R&D buildings near the Middlefield light rail station with a neighborhood of up to 1,900 homes, about 1.3 million sq ft of offices, shops and nearly 10 acres of parks, within Mountain View's East Whisman Precise Plan area.

program.notes: Adopted plan capacity: 4,500 homes and up to 106,000 sq ft of retail. Open space: 5 acres of public parkland plus 5 acres of privately owned open space. A plan amendment in preparation would add 1,500 homes and about 20,000 sq ft of retail, 20,000 sq ft of co-working space and a 10,000 sq ft daycare. projects.name: Esmeralda
projects.acresNote: The Planning Commission staff report (Oct 1, 2026, p. 1) puts the Plan Area at about 261.44 acres east of Asti Road and U.S. 101; it excludes a roughly 4-acre unincorporated strip (the Panhandle), so it is smaller than the 266 to 267 acres in earlier materials and in the 2003 CEQA filing. The draft master tentative map covers 266.84 acres. The 80-foot SMART rail corridor through the site is excluded from the land-use districts.

program.notes: Proposed maximums from the draft Esmeralda Specific Plan development budget (Table 2-3): 605 homes (236 detached single-family, 169 attached condominium or rental, 200 senior living), 160 hotel rooms (up to 30 may be hotel-run residences), 14,000 sq ft spa, 17,300 sq ft retail outside the hotel, 18,400 sq ft office and co-working, 8,000 sq ft light industrial or maker space and 8,000 sq ft preschool or daycare; a K–6 school (up to 200 students) and a 500-seat amphitheater would each need a later use permit. Hotel floor area is not capped. About 162 acres of publicly accessible open space, including a 4.75-acre public sports park to be dedicated to the City. The draft development agreement has the developer pay an inclusionary housing in-lieu fee (about $2.9 million at full build-out) instead of building affordable units on site. The approved but unbuilt Alexander Valley Resort plan it would replace allowed a hotel, spa and golf course, over 100,000 sq ft of commercial uses and up to 235 low-density homes. The City's EIR addendum estimates up to 1,524 new residents. Its eight build-out phases (2027–2036) are estimates, not guaranteed dates; site preparation and the resort-hotel phase must come first, and the development agreement would run 20 years.

projects.name: The Portal (Downtown Rail Extension)
aliases: Transbay Downtown Rail Extension Project, Phase 2
projects.acresNote: A rail line, not a site: a 1.3-mile tunnel from Fourth and King to the Salesforce Transit Center, 2.2 miles of total construction including trackwork in Caltrain's Fourth and King railyard (TJPA, 2026). No official footprint acreage was found. The 2018 Final SEIS/EIR gave longer lengths (2.7 miles with a turnback track at Mariposa Street, 2 miles without it), which have since been superseded. Approximate center is the midpoint of the traced alignment (tunnel and train box) in data/lines/the-portal.geojson.

program.notes: A transit project, so the building program fields do not apply. Scope: a mostly underground rail extension along Townsend and Second Streets, built by cut-and-cover and mined tunneling. It includes a new underground Fourth and Townsend Street Station (two tracks, a center platform and two side platforms, serving Caltrain), the fit-out of the existing two-level train box under the Salesforce Transit Center (six tracks and three center platforms for Caltrain and high-speed rail), ventilation and emergency exit structures, and trackwork in Caltrain's Fourth and King railyard. The 2026 scope changes removed the high-speed rail platforms at Fourth and Townsend, the train box extension and the intercity bus facility. They also shortened the tunnel stub box by about 750 feet. Project budget: $8.255 billion in year-of-expenditure dollars (2023 estimate, including the completed train box, contingency and financing). The 2025 updated estimate is about $7.572 billion, and TJPA holds the difference as unallocated contingency. FTA's Capital Investment Grant share is $3.38 billion. TJPA's July 2026 funding plan lists $1,304 million committed from non-CIG sources, $1,303 million in planned state funds, $265 million in other planned sources and $729 million already invested in the train box, which leaves a $587 million gap. TJPA forecasts over 125,000 average daily riders.

projects.developer: Transbay Joint Powers Authority (TJPA), lead agency

projects.stageNote: Environmentally cleared and in the Engineering phase of FTA's Capital Investment Grants program since May 2024, but not yet under construction or fully funded. Design is at 30% for the tunnel and stations and 60% for the early works. Right-of-way appraisals are under way, and proposals for the civil and tunnel progressive design-build contract are due Oct 9, 2026. The Full Funding Grant Agreement is targeted for July 2027. TJPA says utility relocation construction will start in 2028 and forecasts that the line will be ready for service on Nov 17, 2036.

projects.summary: A rail tunnel to bring Caltrain, and later high-speed rail, from the Fourth and King terminus about 1.3 miles into the Salesforce Transit Center, whose two-level underground train box was built for it and has stood empty since 2018. It adds an underground station at Fourth and Townsend. The $8.3 billion project is environmentally cleared and in federal engineering review, with a $3.38 billion federal grant in sight. It still needs the rest of its local and state funding, and TJPA forecasts service in late 2036.

projects.name: California High-Speed Rail: San Francisco to San Jose
aliases: San Francisco to San Jose Project Section
HSR blended system on the Caltrain corridor
projects.city: San Francisco to San Jose (Caltrain corridor)
projects.county: San Francisco, San Mateo and Santa Clara
projects.acresNote: A rail line, not a site: about 49 miles of existing Caltrain corridor (48.9 miles of existing track in the Final EIR/EIS) from the Fourth and King station in San Francisco to San Jose Diridon, shared with Caltrain ('blended'). The Board's 2022 approval covers Fourth and King to Scott Boulevard in Santa Clara. The stretch from Scott Boulevard to Diridon and West Alma Avenue was approved with the San Jose to Merced section. No official acreage was found. Approximate center is the midpoint of the drawn line (Fourth and King to San José Diridon) in data/lines/cahsr-sf-sj.geojson.

program.notes: A transit project, so the building program fields do not apply. The approved project (Alternative A) runs high-speed trains on Caltrain's electrified tracks rather than a new dedicated line. It would modify about 17.4 miles of existing track, mostly within the Caltrain right-of-way, add no passing tracks, build a light maintenance facility in East Brisbane and modify eight existing stations or platforms. It would also add safety upgrades at 40 at-grade crossings, 8.8 miles of new fencing and 21 radio towers. High-speed rail stations: Fourth and King in San Francisco (interim, until The Portal brings trains to the Salesforce Transit Center), Millbrae (for SFO and BART) and San Jose Diridon. Gilroy, the next station south, is in the San Jose to Merced section. The Final EIR/EIS (June 2022) estimated the preferred alternative at about $5,317 million in 2021 dollars. The 2026 Business Plan estimates the 'San Francisco to Gilroy Blended Approach' at $1,273 million (year-of-expenditure dollars, San Francisco–Bakersfield scenario; $1,291 million in the Phase 1 scenario). That figure excludes the San Jose to Gilroy upgrades ($2 to $5 billion, a 'shared benefit' project) and The Portal. The Authority contributed $714 million to Caltrain's electrification of the 51 miles between San Francisco and San José, which high-speed trains will share.

projects.developer: California High-Speed Rail Authority, lead agency (CEQA, and NEPA under assignment from the Federal Railroad Administration)
publicPartners: Peninsula Corridor Joint Powers Board (Caltrain), owner and operator of the shared corridor
Transbay Joint Powers Authority (The Portal, to the Salesforce Transit Center)
Federal Railroad Administration (NEPA assignment MOU, July 23, 2019)

projects.stageNote: Environmentally cleared: the Authority's Board certified the Final EIR/EIS and approved the route in August 2022, and the Record of Decision followed in October 2022. No construction has started. The 2026 Business Plan's schedule lists right-of-way, design, and the Fourth and King, Millbrae and San Jose station work as 'not started'. It plans for trains to reach the Bay Area over upgraded shared tracks by 2039 in its San Francisco–Bakersfield scenario. That depends on funding and on agreements with Caltrain and partners, including for the San Jose to Gilroy line. Until The Portal is built, Fourth and King is the interim terminus.

timeline.event: The Authority and the FRA certify the statewide Tier 1 program EIR/EIS for the high-speed rail system.
A second Tier 1 program EIR/EIS covers the Bay Area to Central Valley connection (revised under CEQA in 2012).
The Authority issues the Draft EIR/EIS for the San Francisco to San Jose section.

The Board votes 8–0 to certify the Final EIR/EIS and approve Alternative A from Fourth and King to Scott Boulevard, with the East Brisbane maintenance facility and the Millbrae station design (Resolutions HSRA 22-19, 22-20 and 22-21).

projects.nextMilestone: None scheduled for this section. The 2026 Business Plan shows right-of-way, design, and the Fourth and King, Millbrae and San Jose station work as not started, within a San Francisco–Bakersfield timeline that runs to 2039.
projects.summary: The Bay Area end of California's high-speed rail line. Rather than building new tracks up the Peninsula, high-speed trains would share Caltrain's newly electrified corridor for about 49 miles from San Francisco to San Jose, stopping at Fourth and King (and later the Salesforce Transit Center via The Portal), Millbrae for SFO, and San Jose Diridon. The route was environmentally approved in 2022, but no construction has started and the Authority's current plan reaches the Bay Area by 2039.

projects.acresNote: A rail line, not a site: about 6 miles of extension, about 5 miles of it in a single bored tunnel, from Berryessa/North San José to Santa Clara. No official acreage for the whole footprint was found; the 2002 CEQA notice for the original 16-mile corridor (SCH 2002022004) gives about 250 acres, which is not this phase. Approximate center is the midpoint along the alignment drawn from VTA's GIS layer.

program.notes: A transit project, so the building program fields do not apply. Scope: about 6 miles of BART extension, four stations (28th Street/Little Portugal, Downtown San José and Diridon underground; Santa Clara at grade next to the Santa Clara Caltrain station), a train maintenance and storage facility at Newhall Yard, and 48 BART cars bought through BART's existing contract (estimated $172.6 million). One tunnel about 53 feet across holds both tracks side by side. VTA forecasts 55,000 weekday riders. Budget adopted for FTA's Engineering phase: $12.746 billion (year-of-expenditure dollars), with FTA's share capped at $5.1 billion; VTA's July 2026 funding table shows a $564 million gap still to be filled.

projects.developer: Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority (VTA), project sponsor and owner; BART will operate and maintain it
publicPartners: Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority (lead agency and owner)
Federal Transit Administration (Capital Investment Grants, New Starts)
projects.stageNote: Early construction, ahead of tunneling. Crews finished excavating the West Portal launch structure for the tunnel boring machine in early September 2026, and demolition and utility relocation are under way at station sites. In August 2026 VTA signed a restated tunnel contract and gave notice to proceed with pre-tunneling work only. The federal grant agreement that would fund most of the line is not yet signed (VTA's target is late 2027), the boring machine is in storage in Germany with delivery expected in the second half of 2027, and FTA's oversight consultant rates the project high risk while VTA re-baselines its cost and schedule.

projects.summary: VTA's six-mile extension of BART from Berryessa through downtown San José to Santa Clara, with three underground stations, one at-grade station and a rail yard, built around a single tunnel about 53 feet across. Its adopted budget is $12.7 billion. Early works are under way at the tunnel launch site, but the federal grant that would pay for about 40% of it is not yet signed, and service is scheduled for 2039 (VTA aims for 2037).

projects.name: Diridon Station redevelopment
projects.acresNote: No official acreage for the station project was found. Its planning boundary is the DISC boundary (Alternatives Development Report, Figure 2-1), and the August 2026 Steering Committee materials map a 'Future Station Project Footprint'; neither gives an area. The map draws the August 2026 footprint as far as the slide shows it (about 12 acres as traced, cut at the slide's edges), which is not an official acreage. The Caltrain maintenance facility just north of the station (nearly 13 acres) is kept, not rebuilt. Approximate center is the San Jose Diridon Station parent stop in VTA's GTFS feed.

program.notes: A rebuilt rail station, so the building program fields do not apply. The preferred At-Grade Alternative keeps tracks and platforms at about today's level and digs a new concourse beneath them, with connections down to light rail and the future BART station; it keeps the historic depot and the Annex facade. Conceptual layout: three tracks and two platforms for Union Pacific, Amtrak, ACE and Capitol Corridor, four electrified tracks and two platforms for Caltrain, and three electrified tracks and two platforms for high-speed rail. The concourse level would include over 200,000 sq ft of new retail space. The Diridon Program adds street and rail-crossing work at Park Avenue, San Carlos Street (bridge replacement), Auzerais Avenue (new grade separation), West Virginia Street (closure with a walk-bike undercrossing), Stockton Avenue/The Alameda, and noise barriers. Two partner-owned sites (32 and 60 Stockton Avenue, owned by VTA; 698 W. Santa Clara Street, owned by Caltrain) are to be studied as transit-oriented development. Conceptual cost $3 billion to $6 billion and 7 to 10 years of construction. The surrounding Diridon Station Area Plan (up to 12,900 homes and 14.7 million sq ft of office and commercial space) is a separate city plan and is not counted here.

publicPartners: Diridon Station Steering Committee (decision-making body under the partners' cooperative agreement)
Caltrain / Peninsula Corridor Joint Powers Board (leads engineering and environmental review)
Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority (governance, funding and advocacy)
projects.stageNote: In environmental review. The partner agencies' Steering Committee chose the At-Grade Alternative on May 21, 2025, and the environmental phase began in late 2025 with a three-year, $41 million budget. As of August 2026 the program was still being defined for review (no notice of preparation yet), the committee was backing state legislation (SB 1375) for a CEQA exemption for the station, and a bill to create a construction authority was being drafted for 2027. There is no construction funding.

timeline.event: The City of San José, Caltrain, VTA, the High-Speed Rail Authority and MTC sign a cooperative agreement to plan the new station.
San José's City Council, Caltrain's Board and the High-Speed Rail Authority Board accept the staff-recommended Concept Layout from the Diridon Integrated Station Concept Plan.
The partners sign an updated cooperative agreement, replacing the advisory board with a Steering Committee that has voting authority.
The Diridon Station Steering Committee approves the At-Grade Alternative and the Diridon Program of Projects for environmental review, with a three-year budget for that phase.
San José's Transportation and Environment Committee recommends that the City Council accept the Steering Committee's decision (Council agenda June 10, 2025).
The partners publish the Diridon Station Alternatives Development Report.
The environmental phase begins in the fourth quarter of 2025, with ICF as the partners' environmental consultant.
The Steering Committee votes to support SB 1375, a CEQA exemption for urban intermodal rail stations, and appoints a subcommittee to draft legislation for a construction authority.
The Steering Committee receives the environmental review update: barrier locations and two transit-oriented development sites are added to the program definition.

projects.nextMilestone: Neighborhood meetings on the project definition from September to November 2026 and a community open house in November or December 2026; a final update on the CEQA exemption in fall 2026; a draft construction-authority bill and funding plan in winter 2027, with engineering and technical studies for environmental review to follow. The partners expect environmental review to take three to four years in all.
projects.summary: A plan by five public agencies to rebuild San José's 90-year-old Diridon Station into a hub for Caltrain, high-speed rail, BART, ACE, Capitol Corridor, Amtrak and light rail, keeping the tracks at street level with a new concourse dug beneath them. The partners estimate $3 billion to $6 billion and 7 to 10 years of construction; environmental review has begun, but construction funding has not been found.

projects.name: Valley Link
projects.acresNote: Not applicable: a rail line, not a site. Phase 1A is about 11 miles of new passenger rail along I-580 from the Dublin/Pleasanton BART Station to the Vasco Road ACE Station in Livermore (AB 1171 Initial Project Report, June 10, 2026 board packet, PDF p. 30). Station and facility sites: Isabel Station parking on a 24-acre site, Vasco Road Station on about 13 acres, and the Livermore OMF on the southeastern part of a 13.75-acre site (PDF pp. 32–33).

program.notes: Transit infrastructure; the housing and commercial fields don't apply. Phase 1A: about 11 miles, three stations (Dublin/Pleasanton, an aerial station south of I-580 next to the BART station; Isabel, in the I-580 median in Livermore; Vasco Road, with a cross-platform transfer to ACE), a Livermore operations and maintenance facility, and six battery electric multiple unit (BEMU) trains on 15-minute weekday headways (June 10, 2026 packet, PDF pp. 30–33). Forecast about 16,000 weekday boardings in 2050 (PDF p. 35). Total project budget $2,045.7 million in year-of-expenditure dollars, of which $1,676.4 million is construction and rolling stock (PDF p. 39). The 22-mile Phase 1 to Mountain House, cleared under CEQA (2024) and NEPA (2025), is now Phase 1A plus Phase 1B (Southfront Road to Mountain House, funding to be determined); the 2021 EIR covered a 42-mile, seven-station system to North Lathrop.

projects.stageNote: Environmentally cleared and in design; no construction yet. The Authority certified the Subsequent EIR for the 22-mile Phase 1 in October 2024 and FTA issued a FONSI on May 27, 2025. In June 2025 the Board split delivery after cost increases at 30% design, starting with the 11-mile Phase 1A to Vasco Road; a joint CEQA addendum and NEPA re-evaluation for the 1.5-mile connection from I-580/First Street to Vasco Road is targeted for fall 2026. A CM/GC preconstruction contract went to Kiewit in June 2026. Construction funding is not yet secured: the Authority is preparing to ask FTA to enter the Capital Investment Grants Engineering phase.

timeline.event: The Authority publishes the notice of preparation for an EIR on the Valley Link Rail Project (SCH 2018092027).
The Authority delivers its Project Feasibility Report to the Legislature, as AB 758 requires (final report adopted October 2019).
The Board certifies the Final EIR for a 42-mile, seven-station line from Dublin/Pleasanton BART to North Lathrop, with an initial segment to Mountain House.
The Board adopts the 22-mile Phase 1 alignment to Mountain House, with four stations, as the locally preferred alternative.
The Board certifies the Subsequent EIR and approves the 22-mile Phase 1 project; the notice of determination is filed Oct 25.
FTA issues a Finding of No Significant Impact for Phase 1 under NEPA.
After cost increases at 30% design, the Board approves phased delivery starting with the 11-mile Phase 1A from Dublin/Pleasanton BART to the Vasco Road ACE Station, using battery-electric trains.
The Board chooses Construction Manager/General Contractor delivery for Phase 1A; the request for proposals goes out that month.
Alameda CTC awards $4 million in I-580 toll revenue for Phase 1A final design.
The Board awards Kiewit Infrastructure West a CM/GC preconstruction contract (Tier 1, up to $3 million) and requests MTC bridge toll funds to finish 30% design.
Cumulative MTC funding for project development reaches $53.8 million.

projects.summary: A new passenger rail line along the I-580 corridor linking BART at Dublin/Pleasanton with ACE commuter trains at Vasco Road in Livermore, so riders from the San Joaquin Valley can change trains across a platform instead of driving over the Altamont Pass. The first 11 miles, with three stations and battery-electric trains, are environmentally cleared and in design; an extension to Mountain House is cleared but unfunded.

projects.name: SMART Healdsburg extension
projects.acresNote: A rail line, not a site. The extension runs about 9 miles along SMART's existing right-of-way, from milepost 62.94 near Windsor River Road to milepost 72.00 at Lytton Springs Road and Healdsburg Avenue; the right-of-way is 60 to 250 feet wide (CEQA addendum, Dec 2025, PDF pp. 7 and 18). CEQAnet's Dec 19, 2025 notice for the addendum lists 103 total acres, and the addendum's field surveys covered about 103.5 acres, mostly within SMART's right-of-way (PDF p. 64).

program.notes: Transit infrastructure; the housing and commercial fields don't apply. About 9 miles of Class IV main-line track rebuilt on SMART's out-of-service Northwestern Pacific right-of-way from Windsor to Lytton Springs Road north of Healdsburg, one new station in Healdsburg (the system's fifteenth), a 5.5-mile extension of the SMART Pathway, 21 at-grade crossings, Positive Train Control, station gauntlet tracks for freight, bridge work including replacement of the roughly 565-foot Russian River railroad bridge in the same location, and dispatch and broadband upgrades (CTC baseline agreement, PDF pp. 5 and 30; CEQA addendum, PDF pp. 24 and 26). Cost estimate $268,749,000, which SMART and the CTC describe as fully funded: TIRCP $34.8 million (cycles 3 and 6) and $81 million (cycle 7), SCCP $56 million, LPP competitive $25 million, Regional Measure 3 $40 million, FRA CRISI $28.14 million, Sonoma County Measure M $2 million and FTA Community Project Funding $1.8 million (baseline agreement, Dec 2025, PDF p. 37; CTC, Jan 2026). In June 2026 the CTC added $207,000 in LPP formulaic funds for construction (Resolution LPP-P-2526-17). A $6 million zero-emission switcher locomotive is funded alongside it. Delivered by progressive design-build; the Phase I agreement with Stacy and Witbeck/Herzog, a joint venture, was awarded for $21,754,398.54 on Sept 17, 2025 and amended on Aug 19, 2026 to $22,506,169.82, adding design work paid for by the City of Healdsburg and the County of Sonoma.

projects.developer: Sonoma-Marin Area Rail Transit District (SMART; implementing agency and CEQA lead agency)
publicPartners: California Transportation Commission (SCCP and LPP funds; allocates TIRCP funds; CEQA responsible agency)
Sonoma County Transportation and Climate Authority (Measure M)
Federal Railroad Administration (CRISI grant; categorical exclusion for the systems work)
projects.stageNote: Funded, environmentally cleared and in design; construction hasn't started. The route is covered by SMART's 2006 EIR and 2008 SEIR for the 70-mile system; the Board adopted an addendum for this segment on Dec 17, 2025, and the California Transportation Commission, as a responsible agency, accepted it and approved the project for future consideration of funding on Jan 29, 2026. The progressive design-build team, under contract since September 2025, had prepared 50% design documents by September 2026, and utility potholing began in April 2026. The first construction package, Windsor Station to Front Street, is due for award in October 2026, with construction starting in spring 2027; a second package, Front Street to North Street, includes the station. SMART is also asking the public where the Healdsburg station should go: the historic Depot/Hudson Street site the City prefers (reaffirmed in September 2026), or a Downtown site on Vine Street about 0.45 mile away. Service is planned for December 2028.

projects.summary: The next step north for SMART's trains: about nine miles of railroad, idle for decades, rebuilt from today's end of the line at Windsor through Healdsburg, with a new Healdsburg station, a replacement Russian River rail bridge and the SMART Pathway alongside. It is funded at about $269 million, in design, and planned to open in late 2028; where the Healdsburg station goes is being reconsidered.

projects.name: SMART Cloverdale extension
projects.acresNote: Not applicable: a rail line, not a site. SMART's 2025-2030 Strategic Plan describes the extension as 13.5 miles of rail and pathway from Lytton Springs Road to 1st Street in Cloverdale (PDF p. 33), along SMART's existing railroad right-of-way, which SMART owns north to milepost 89.0 in Cloverdale (Aug 19, 2026 packet, PDF p. 244).

program.notes: Transit infrastructure; the housing and commercial fields don't apply. Rail and pathway on SMART's out-of-service right-of-way from Lytton Springs Road, where the funded Healdsburg extension ends, to 1st Street in Cloverdale: 13.5 miles in the 2025-2030 Strategic Plan (PDF p. 33); SMART's June 2026 staff report puts Healdsburg to Cloverdale at about 18 miles (Aug 19, 2026 packet, PDF p. 85). Two new stations: Geyserville, which the Board adopted on Aug 19, 2026 for a site at 255 Highway 128 near Remmel Road, about halfway, and Cloverdale, whose location SMART lists as to be determined. Plan Bay Area 2050+ lists the extension at $353 million in capital cost and $63 million in operating cost (year-of-expenditure dollars), opening in 2025-2035 (PDF p. 42); the Strategic Plan carried it as $401.7 million in pending grants (PDF p. 43). No construction funding is secured.

projects.developer: Sonoma-Marin Area Rail Transit District (SMART; project sponsor)
publicPartners: Caltrans (US 101 North Comprehensive Multimodal Corridor Plan)
projects.stageNote: Shown as proposed: environmentally cleared but not yet fully funded, with no construction schedule; SMART says the Cloverdale station will be completed when funding becomes available. SMART's 2006 EIR and 2008 SEIR covered the whole 70-mile corridor to Cloverdale. On Aug 19, 2026 the Board adopted a Geyserville station into SMART's program and approved it as a station project of its own, statutorily exempt from CEQA as a passenger rail project (Public Resources Code 21080.25, as amended by SB 71), to be advanced as part of the extension to Cloverdale; SMART filed the notice of exemption the next day. The extension is in Plan Bay Area 2050+, adopted in March 2026, with a $353 million capital cost and a 2025-2035 opening period, but SMART says it still needs state and federal grants and has applications pending or in development. SMART puts Healdsburg to Cloverdale at about 18 miles, and a Geyserville station at about the midpoint lets it split that into two smaller projects that may compete better for grants. The Cloverdale station site is listed as to be determined, and the Healdsburg design-build contract includes options to continue north if more grants are secured.

projects.summary: The last leg of the voter-approved SMART system: about 13.5 miles of out-of-service railroad from north of Healdsburg to Cloverdale, with new stations at Geyserville (adopted in August 2026) and Cloverdale. It was environmentally cleared with the rest of the line and is in the regional plan, but it has no construction funding yet.

projects.name: Mission Bay Ferry Landing

projects.acresNote: A ferry landing, not a development site. The Final Mitigated Negative Declaration lists the Port lots 9900/064 and 9900/064H with a lot size of 153,257 sq ft (cover page); the landing itself is a pier of about 108 by 22 ft, a 26 by 22 ft connecting ramp, an 85 by 10 ft gangway and a 135 by 42 ft float (Table 1, p. 5).

program.notes: Transit infrastructure; the housing and commercial fields don't apply. A single-float, two-berth ferry landing in the Bay at Terry A. Francois Boulevard, about 100 ft south of 16th Street, with a covered pier, gangway, guide and fender piles, a Ferry Landing Plaza, improvements to Agua Vista Park and connections to the emergency firefighting water system. The Port says it can handle up to 6,000 passengers a day (May 2025). San Francisco Bay Ferry (WETA) is building the float as an electric charging float for battery-electric ferries; service is planned to the Downtown San Francisco Ferry Building, with special-event service to Chase Center. Phase 2B construction contract: $33,018,200 (plus a $3,301,820 contingency), funded by Port capital ($640,000), the 2012 GO bond ($2 million), the SFPUC ($4 million), a UCSF grant ($2.5 million), the SF sales tax ($4.5 million), Regional Measure 3 ($13.86 million) and an EPA grant ($5,518,200). The Board of Supervisors says the SFCTA's $4.5 million grant leverages more than $75.8 million from other local, state and federal sources for the landing. WETA's FY2026/27 capital budget carries $39.1 million for its Mission Bay electrification project.

projects.acresNote: Planning Commission Motion 20493 (2019): a 114,048 sq ft (2.61-acre) lot, Assessor's Block 3786, Lot 037, with frontages on Brannan, 5th and Bluxome streets. Planning's 2025 record: an approximately 2.6-acre development lot to be split into parcels of 43,670, 47,580 and 22,690 sq ft.

program.notes: As approved on Dec 12, 2025 (Planning record 2025-004642PRJ): the lot is split into three parcels. Two high-rise residential buildings, about 1,777,000 sq ft in all, go on the western (43,670 sq ft) and central (47,580 sq ft) parcels: the western one 599 ft tall with 785 homes in about 914,000 sq ft, including a 2,035 sq ft ground-floor commercial space; the eastern one 528 ft tall with 715 homes in about 863,000 sq ft. 1,500 rental homes in all (459 studios, 655 one-bedroom, 343 two-bedroom, 33 three-bedroom), 150 of them affordable to low-income households per Planning's record, which lists the project as using the State Density Bonus. Each building has four levels of parking (465 spaces in all) and there are 450 bike spaces. The easternmost parcel (22,690 sq ft) is to be dedicated to the City for future affordable housing, and the project builds the Bluxome Linear Park along the north side of Bluxome Street between 4th and 5th streets. The site's earlier approval (Motion 20493, 2019, modified in 2023) is for an office project of about 1.2 million sq ft with 775,000 sq ft of office.

projects.name: Berkeley Space Center
aliases: Berkeley Air & Space Center at NASA Research Park
Berkeley Space Center at NASA Research Park
projects.acresNote: The joint Final EIR/EIS (Aug 2026, p. 2-4) gives an approximately 39-acre Project Site, plus about 6 acres of off-site utility and demolition work (45 acres in all). The 2024 notice of preparation described a 36-acre site, the size of the 2020 Enhanced Use Lease (p. 2-3); the leased parcel boundary measures 34.92 acres (p. 2-28). The site line traced from the project's land use plan measures 39.3 acres.

program.notes: Maximums for the CEQA Proposed Project (NEPA Build Alternative 1), about 2.32 million sq ft in all (Final EIR/EIS Table 2-3): 2,000,000 sq ft of research and office uses (350,000 office, 1,390,000 lab and R&D, 260,000 academic), a 25,000 sq ft conference center, 90,000 sq ft of publicly accessible active uses (retail, food, maker space and similar), 130,000 sq ft of student and faculty housing (about 145 units, used by UC students and faculty for a semester to an academic year; at least 10 percent affordable at 80 percent of area median income) and 75,000 sq ft of short-term lodging (about 100 units), plus two parking garages. At least 10 acres of publicly accessible open space, around a Central Green. Buildings up to 80 ft (30 ft in the Central Green), with up to 25 ft more for mechanical screens. The Reduced Density Alternative (NEPA Build Alternative 2) has 1.08 million sq ft of research and office uses (1.4 million sq ft in all) and could also be approved; a variant would replace the housing with 130,000 sq ft of research space.

projects.developer: Moffett Partners, LLC (a joint venture of the UC Regents and SKSP NRP, LLC; SKS Partners is its development manager)
publicPartners: NASA Ames Research Center (landowner under an Enhanced Use Lease; NEPA lead agency and final decision-maker)
The Regents of the University of California (CEQA lead agency; joint venture partner)
projects.stageNote: In review. On Sept 16, 2026 the University of California, as CEQA lead agency, authorized Moffett Partners to submit the project to NASA, adopting CEQA findings, a statement of overriding considerations and a mitigation monitoring and reporting program. NASA, which owns the land, is the final decision-maker: it must still issue a Record of Decision under NEPA and approve the project before it issues construction permits. No NASA decision could be checked as of Oct 19, 2026.

timeline.event: NASA completes a programmatic environmental impact statement and Record of Decision for the NASA Ames Development Plan, which includes the NASA Research Park where the site lies.
NASA invites the UC Regents to explore developing the site for research, professional education and housing.
The UC Regents and NASA enter into an Enhanced Use Lease for about 36 acres in the NASA Research Park.
The UC Regents authorize UC Berkeley to form a joint venture with SKSP NRP, LLC, creating Moffett Partners, LLC, for the project.
The Enhanced Use Lease is assigned to an affiliate of Moffett Partners, LLC.
UC Berkeley issues the notice of preparation for a joint EIR/EIS with NASA (SCH 2024060942); NASA's notice of intent follows on June 26, 2024.
UC Berkeley and NASA release the joint Draft EIR/EIS for public review through June 10, 2026.
UC Berkeley and NASA publish the joint Final EIR/EIS.

The University of California authorizes submittal of the project to NASA for its review and approval, with CEQA findings, a statement of overriding considerations and a mitigation program; the notice of determination is filed the next day.

projects.nextMilestone: NASA's Record of Decision on the project. The Final EIR/EIS plans construction in four phases from 2027 to 2040, with the first buildings occupied in 2032.
projects.summary: A research campus planned by Moffett Partners, a joint venture of the UC Regents and SKSP NRP, on about 39 acres of federal land at NASA Ames Research Center beside Hangar One, under a 2020 lease from NASA. It would add up to 2.3 million sq ft, mostly labs and offices, with a conference center, about 145 student and faculty housing units, about 100 short-term lodging units and a Central Green. The University approved sending the project to NASA in September 2026; NASA makes the final decision.
